subs.title: Big-O for loops, nested loops, halving and extra storage

c.v: Big-O describes how the work grows as the input grows, ignoring constant factors. O(n) means the work is at most a constant times n once n is large. In an interview, always give
time and extra space, and name the variables: "O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space, where n is the number of intervals."
How to derive it from code:

items.v: Code in sequence: add, then keep the largest term.
A loop over n followed by a loop over n is O(n + n) = O(n).
A loop over n inside a loop over m is O(n·m). If the inner loop runs i times for i = 0 … n−1, the total is n(n−1)/2, which is O(n²).
A loop where i doubles, or n halves, runs about log₂ n times. That's binary search's cost.
keep both variables. O(n + m) and O(n·m) are different answers; don't collapse them to n.
is the memory beyond the input: new containers, the output if you build it, and the recursion stack, whose depth counts.
